review:
Sometimes, second impressions are more important than the first...

I picked this game up last year, not long after finally playing "Divine Divinity", which quickly became a favorite of mine, due to the off-kilter writing, challenging and free-form battles, and stellar atmosphere and audio. With all the buzz around the latest Divinity and overwhelmingly positive reviews, I finally plunked down the premium price for the game, and entered a world of initial disappointment: The complex mechanics, challenging difficulty , and voice acting that comes out of all corners, on top of convoluted quests seemed to be a bit too much for me at the time. I put several hours into the game and then shelved it, rather disappointed. I couldn't see how the game received such overwhelming reviews with what a mess it seemed to be at the time. Fast forward about a year later, and I give it another whirl, just on a hunch...that maybe, just maybe I'd be able to find it more palatable this time. I'm sure glad I gave it another go. After reading up a bit more on the game's mechanics and stats, I started with an open mind and a brand new character. I decided to devote a good four or five hours into my first session back and really get a good undertstanding of what's going on, and that's when it just *clicked* for me. The attention to every detail, every line in conversation, every battle, every creature, scroll, skill book, ingredient and object you can interact with is unparalleled. This game gives me the same feeling I got when playing Ultima VI and Wizardry V back in the day...you want to keep exploring, learning, experimenting, and not stop playing. I'm 40 years old and have many responsibilities in life, yet I've found "Divinity: Original Sin" keeping me up until the wee hours of the morning, going to work exhausted, telling myself "I'll take a break from it tonight", but going back to play again and again. I've put about 30 hours into this play through so far and I feel I'm just scratching the surface. The writing takes some of the fantasy stereotypes and rewrites them in such a way that makes them unpredictable. Once you understand the battle mechanics and the different ways you can win a fight, it becomes very rewarding. Plenty of loot in the game, even the seemingly useless items can obtain value by crafting or sellling for a few extra gold pieces. Speaking of selling: most random NPC's you can trade with, which is a great touch: just like in real life, most people will have some sort of currency or item you'd want. Digging graves, making traps explode, talking with animals, setting random things on fire, breaking into inn rooms, the list of things to do goes on and on...and unlike a lot of RPG's, none of it feels like "filler" or busy work. I'm very much looking forward to checking out the sequel when it's officially released in later 2017. For now, I see "Divinity: OSEE" keeping me plenty of busy, and rewarded, until that time.

Divinity: Original Sin feels like an old-school tabletop campaign where the DM says “yes” to everything and then quietly waits for you to ruin it.
The combat is dense, systems-driven, and gloriously unforgiving, demanding attention, planning, and the willingness to reload after one wrong step.
It’s not smooth, it’s not modern, but it has soul, the kind that only CRPGs with too many mechanics and too much confidence can have.
Finished it at 100%. 100% complete. No regrets. (Some regrets.)

I played Divinity: Original Sin 2 first, and it is a better game I'd say, but Divinity: Original Sin 1 is still a good game. 

If you've exhausted your playtime on Divinity: Original Sin 2 and want more (and lament that BG3 is not ready yet), you may like this game. In my points, I will compare a lot to D:OS2 to give you the "feel".

Pro: 

+ Combat is fun. It's the best part of the game.

+ Everything is voiced. I might not really care what they have to say most of the time and skip the convos, but I greatly appreciate the fact that it is there (for Enhanced Edition).

+ Graphics is pretty good for CRPG and everything is colourful. Easy on the eyes. I don't feel depressed while playing, unlike when I play other games where everything is grey.

Bad:

- The animations (particularly the combat animations) and sound effects feel much more sluggish and slow compared to D:OS2 (where it felt very snappy and articulated). I recommend downloading a mod speeding up the combat animations slightly. 

- because of the above mentioned, healing out of combat is slow af. There are no Bedrolls to instaheal you out of combat like in D:OS2. I recommend a mod that gives you a full heal potion that you can only use out of combat to mitigate this annoyance. 

- There is a lot of moving around and going back and forth (backtracking) particularly in the first area (Cyseal). I recommend a mod that increases your party's run speed slightly.

- The puzzles are fine, and I didn't have problems solving them on my own (there are often multiple ways to solve them). However, there are several times where the only solution is to find a teeny tiny button somewhere that I failed to find even with extremely high Perception stat on my character. I had to google where it is after I got tired of pixel searching for one hour. Oh, and did I mention there are several of these?




Other Thoughts:

* Combat is more traditional/RNG based than D:OS2. Don't worry though becasue RNG still feels secondary to your tactics.

* The soundtrack has a very whimsical feel compared to D:OS2. (RIP composer dude)

* The tone is very wacky/humorous and light. Personally I like it that way than being overly serious because it makes it easy to digest.

* The story is meh. Some might enjoy it, but I didn't care for it at all (there is a lot of "tell" via dialogue and little "show"), but I still had fun because of the combat. The D:OS2 story felt much more organic because it wasn't told mostly through some character talking nonstop while standing still (ahem).

* There are companions, but they're pretty forgettable (you'll probably only care about their stats than their personal story or whatever, even if you're the type of person that likes stories and lore). D:OS2 definitely improved on this.

* Crafting is kind of important in this game. The weapons and gear (particularly the weapons) you craft are vastly superior to the ones you loot.

* That being said, you'll probably spend a ton of time looking inside your bags..

* Unlike D:OS2 where you could respec yourself and your companions for free infinite number of times, you can only respec yourself (the two source hunters) after the game's mid-point. Also respeccing will cause that character to lose/forget all of their spells, so you'll have to buy and relearn all of the skill books again.

After playing BG3, which is a great game btw. Hope it wins GOTY. Anw, I decided to visit Larian's roots to see what makes BG3 such a good game, and hence found DOS1 (gonna start DOS2 soon). Am a big fan of open world, CRPG, RPG, so it's a no-brainer to buy this game if you're fans of those genres.

<My first hour, with Mors Gotha:>

Customized two characters for my party.  Appreciated the graphics and turn based combat, which has substantial depth.  Had to restart and lower it to "normal" difficulty.  Did the tutorial dungeon, some nice physics (you can burn out poison clouds with fire, throw covers on gas grates).  Made it to the first town.  I have a letter of introduction, but the two gate guards are illiterate and won't let us in. AI Player #2 Mors Gotha (the antagonist of Ultima Underworld 2 and a name that I've used for years) is set to "rascal" personality and insists we attack the guards for insulting us.  I caution against it, and lose a few rounds of scissor rock paper.  She wins and attacks the guards.  We defeat them and enter town.  Suddenly orcs attack.... during the battle, I hear townspeople yelling for the missing guards by name.  After the battle, I return to the scene of the crime and notice another legionairre examining their bodies and asking what happened to them.  I say nothing.  

Currently talking to a couple guards, one who has a love-potion-charmed-feral-orc as a girlfriend, I'm voting we let love take it's course, Mors is saying it's not permanent she tried a potion on me without any luck.  Despite putting a point into Charm to make me better at scissor, rock, paper -- Mors Gotha wins again.  And we bash the orc's head in and she dies.  The guard runs away crying.  I'd say it's off to a good start.

<Halfway or so thru: The continuing misadventures of Mors Gotha, the Good Idea Fairy:>

I'm now hooked.  Bottom line is it may very reminiscent of the feel of the Ultima series, which was my favorite growing up (I did play the 2002 Divinity and liked it and thought it was well written, but this is far better).  I liked this game enough that I bought part 2 during the Christmas sale and plan on playing it next.  I like the combat -- although I tell myself I like "turn based," I find most games far too inferior to X-Com 2 to be fun.  Not here.  This combat here is pretty tactical, there are alot of options and possible outcomes and I like the fights.  The AI seems pretty good, I've seen a lone unit run to another squad and I've seen them use environmental effects against me. But they also aren't omniscient enough to know I'm immune to Frost and try freezing me (which is fine).  The game looks good on big screen and is optimized for controller (the only negative is to  hide helmets you have to log in once as keyboard, took me half the game to find that out). 

I'll skip plot points but I like the story so far, and you effectively have your own base you can build up.  I also like that although it's a D&D variant system, it's not so alien I feel like I have to learn a new language just to play.  There is some nuance to it and making the builds you want, but I got the hang of it.  Also, it may be the best videogame voice acting I've ever heard -- I rarely skip through the speech.

And about that Mors Gotha, although I have +Charm items and statpoints to make it easier to win at scissor rock paper (currently 6 to her 2 points), she occassionally wins.  She is almost always the Bad Idea Fairy.  Like the original murder of the city guards, when she wins I just let her win and see where the game takes me.  She insisted on guessing the obviously wrong answer to a riddle, and we had to kill the mushroom ring riddlekeepers.  She turned down the "thieves guild" type missions in Silverglen.  Just now she insisted on beating a talking chicken to death, for basically no good reason.  The ones I overrule her on are funny too, no Mors lets not beat the crying Orc to death and take his dead brother's burial armor.  It probably sucks anyway, Mors.  She occassionally agrees without argument, so it's not that she's always deliberately contrarian (loading confirms this, she just has opinions) -- but it's a neat game element that I've never quite seen like this. 

A+, all around.  Why haven't I played this sooner?

Divinity: Original Sin is a roleplaying game developed by Larian Studios. The game was also partially funded through Kickstarter. This enhanced edition of the game was released in October 2015 for PC, PS4 and Xbox One. It came as a free upgrade for everyone that owned the original game which was released in June 2014. 

Gameplay in Original Sin follows a very classic RPG style of play. You control two heroes, and you take part in battles which are turn-based combat.  The game play is very tactical, and some fights can last up to about forty five minutes at times. Positioning, making sure you use potions and spells at the optimal moment all play a key role to success in Original Sin. The combat system can be considered to be slow paced, but I personally enjoyed the tactical thought you have to put into every action you take. The game’s tutorial system at the start of the game is done very well, and introduces all elements of gameplay in a satisfying manner.  A lot of the game is based in dialogue as well; I will say this now, if you aren’t one for reading masses amount of text (or listening to), then you will probably want to avoid playing this game, as there is a boat load of text and dialogue to be found here. There are times when you get to make key choices in the dialogue scenes, and also offers branches to find out more information about lore and plot as well.  Overall, the gameplay is really well done, and if you want to find a game that you can absolutely get completely lost in its gameplay, then you should stop here and just pick it up. 

Graphically, Original Sin looks gorgeous. The enhanced version of the game improved the graphics quite a bit over the original release, and how managed to reduce the install size. The colourful environments and lush greenery just look amazing. This is one of the best looking games I have played in a very long while. The animations of all characters is done very well too; never did I see any janky looking movements or action, which helped at keeping me fully immersed in the beautiful world. 

As with all RPG games, the story is crucial to the reception it gets. Original Sin does not disappoint here either. On top of the games over arching main story line, you also have the chance to branch off into other lesser side plots which can sometimes make you forget all about the rest of the game as they are so in depth. The side quests in this game would probably be main stories in another; that is how good the plot behind Original Sin is. You will of course have to be up for reading the text if you want to get the full effect out of it though. 

The majority of Original Sin is voice acted – this helps a lot given the amount of text in the game, but there are parts, which are sometimes quite randomly selected, which aren’t voice acted. This is where you will need the patience to continue reading the dialogue to fully understand what is happening in the world. The sound effects and soundtrack are really good too; nothing seemed out of place so it fits in well with the game. 

I found the game to be fairly tricky, I had never played the classic RPG games, I was just too young to understand them, and so I felt as if this game took me on a crash course of learning about them. I have to admit, I did have to use wiki’s and FAQs at times to progress and work out how best to tackle a few bosses; but that should be taken as part and parcel of the gaming experience with something of this size. Researching the best action to take for me makes the game all that more fun. 

The world in which this game is set in, feels so alive and active. When you are in towns you can hear plenty of market sellers in the background selling their goods, you can find countless amounts of side quests, and plenty of items to interact with and loot. If you are looking for a game with almost perfect level design, look no further. 

In total, this game took me about 54 hours to complete, this was with doing as many side quests as I could find and listening/reading to all the dialogue in the game as well – that is on single player. Where Original Sin gets above other games of its type, is that you can also play the game in co-op mode as well; that alone means you can probably hit the triple figures for the amount of hours on offer in this game.  There is an absurd amount of content to see. 

Since this is the enhanced edition of the game, I didn’t find any technical issues. The game runs like a dream on 4k resolutions. Loading times are almost none existent as well. Like I said above, they have somehow managed to get the install size down on the game as well, which is something of a mystery given the amount of improvements they have added/changed. .

To sum up, Divinity: Original Sin is an absolute masterpiece of a game. The gameplay whilst slow paced is so well done, it will keep you interested and wanting more after you first battle. The plot is one of the best I have ever had the pleasure of seeing in any video game, and one that I will remember for a very long time. On top of all this, you the amount of content on offer is amazing. I cannot recommend Divinity Original Sin enough, even if you aren’t a massive fan of the RPG genre, this could be the game that changes that opinion for you.

This was on my wishlist forever and when I finally played the game it was worth every penny. It is a really fun modern, tongue-in-cheek, turn based RPG. You create 2 characters to start off with and end up recruiting 2 more as your party battle to save the world.

Two key points to note are:
- This game does not take itself seriously at all. If you want a straight faced, deep plot then look elsewhere.
- This game does not hold your hand. You must be willing to experiment and discover things by yourself (or consult a wiki!)

Turn based RPG veterans will find the default difficulty a bit easy. Tactician mode is recommended.
 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
+ Lots and lots of silly humour - you get to talk to animals and help Walter McWishing Well look for his brother :) 
+ Fun and tactical turn-based combat
+ Streamlined but interesting character development system, giving you plenty of choice to customise your party
+ Crafting system allows you to buff/enhance items and create entirely new ones
+ Challenging puzzles
+ Co-op mode available as well as single player
+ Full voice acting on every single line of dialogue makes the game very immersive. An impressive amount of work must have gone into this.
+ The enhanced edition lives up to its name with smooth, polished and bug free gameplay
+ Pretty graphics and rotatable camera

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
- The pacing of the game feels slightly off. The beginning town of Cyceal could do with more hints to ease the player into the game. At times I ran around not quite sure what to do. The mid game has a few too many trash mobs with little variety. The end game has a section which is full of puzzles, one after the other - I found that a bit exhausting.
- NPCs repeat their lines far too often and it gets irritating. Luckily there is a mod that fixes this - I highly recommend QuietDayOnTheMarket mod by Abraxas1990 [url=http://www.nexusmods.com/divinityoriginalsin/mods/74/?]http://www.nexusmods.com/divinityoriginalsin/mods/74/?[/url] Also check out the FastMoveSpeed mod if you are impatient.
- Inventory gets cluttered with lots of junk items that are useless. 
- The game does not hold your hand. If you love to experiment and spend time trying out different crafting combinations, you will love this. I personally got annoyed by all the undocumented crafting combinations that were available. I highly recommend the use of a wiki to save time.
- The game does not tell you that in order to advance the plot, you need to use certain quest items. Also you must save a certain amount of quest items to succeed near the end of the game. (Trying to avoid spoilers!).
- The storyline is not the greatest so don't expect anything mindblowing.
- One particular area in the game felt slightly unfinished (Sacred Stone I'm looking at you!). Trying to be heroic resulted in reputation loss.
- Insta-kill traps and forced stealth sequences were a bit annoying.

If you have any interest in RPGs you NEED to check this game out. Divinity Original Sin 2 is on my wishlist :)

[b]Short Review: [/b] Easily one of the richest, deepest, best turn-based CRPG's of all time. 

[b]Long Version: [/b]

Like a lot of RPG's, this game can be very unforgiven to new players. The combat can be brutal in the beginning and the game doesn't hold your hand when it comes to quests. You're going to need to summon your best old-school RPG wits and stubbornness to proceed. You will die a lot. Resurrection scrolls are to be used liberally. No joke. 

Character progression, like all the best RPG's, offers so many options and so much depth that gimping yourself is totally possible, and indeed, probable. You're going to want to respec one of your two main characters (if not both) at some point. It's okay: the game offers a chance about 2/3rds of the way through. You'll probably want to play through the game a second time with "perfect" builds all planned and plotted out just so you can see how your ideal builds will work. That's the kind of game this is - your character builds are going to consume a lot of time in planning. 

I will repeat: The game doesn't hold your hand. A lot of quests require you to find some obscure, hidden item, scroll or key. You're going to probably spend a fair amount of time checking Google in order to progress. That's okay. It's a throwback to old-school RPG's. Be persistent. Be relentless. 

Combat in this game is amazingly fun, especially once you get a few levels under your belt and have a few skills and spells to throw around. It's turn based and very tactical; it rewards people who want to think strategically and micro-manage each and every decision. Positioning matters. Playing a rogue is incredibly fun because of this. This is one of those games where a single, well-placed spell (like an Ice Wall) can turn the tide of a battle. The combat reminds me a lot of "The Temple of Elemental Evil" which was also really fun and about as good as turn-based combat gets. 

Quick-save often. You're going to reload quite a bit in the early stages of the game. But eventually you'll get comfortable with everything and get into a groove and your plucky band of heros will start to show their strength. 

The game is huge; bigger than you realize. There's a lot of neat areas, tons of quests (like a good RPG should have) and a lot of interesting characters. Everyone is fully voice-acted and the dialog is often quite cheeky. If you're into that sort of thing you'll find the game very funny at times. 

The art is fun and fanciful and the game is loaded with great looking boss monsters. There are some epic battles. 

I'm a big fan of CRPG's like "Baldur's Gate 2", "Pillars of Eternity" and "The Temple of Elemental Evil". This game easily ranks right up there with the best of them. Fun, engaging, and appeals to the character/class builder in me. Figuring out the optimum build for my characters took some time, but it was totally worth it. 

This is definitely one of the great RPG's.

One of my closest friends and I met 25 years ago playing Dungeons and Dragons together.  We were looking for a co-op RPG experience to have some fun remotely during quarantine, and within the first hour of playing this game we both agreed it couldn't have been any more perfect.  We did character creation together, and then embarked on our quest.  We were delighted at every turn.  The rule set is very true to DnD, the co-op dialog mechanics make it feel like it was created for multi-player and not just bolted on after the fact onto a single player game, and there were moments we've experienced already that worked out perfectly with the two of us working in tandem.  As a 41 year old lifelong gamer it takes a lot to get me pumped about games these days, but this is a true delighter and a true surprise experience I wasn't expecting.

I feel like this game is very underrated when compared to Original Sin 2 and Baldur's Gate 3. Those games are great, but the first Divinity: Original Sin still holds up as well. I heavily recommend playing this game co-op with a dedicated partner, as it has more co-op mechanics than Larian's other titles have, such as mechanics for making decisions as a group (which can get a little awkward when you play singleplayer, because you can end up arguing with yourself), and the fact that you always create two characters (even in singleplayer), and the story revolves around them both.

[b] 8 / 10 --- [/b]  I'm being a little bit harsh given that so many reviewers say it's the best game ever....this *is* a great game but has several very frustrating features.  If you can see past them, there is a very enjoyable and rewarding RPG to be found.  

 [b] The good ---  [/b] 1.  Cool and flexible character design.  As your character evolves you can give them any skill or stat and make them multifaceted.  I taught my tank to learn limited spellcasting abilities so she could self-heal, Vampiric touch, etc. without having to invest more than a couple of points in Intelligence (all of which came from gear).
2.  Super fun to play!  Interesting and interactive skills in a 3-D dynamic turn-based environment.  Rush in and knock down opponents, electrify water at their feet, drop a barrel of oil on their head then throw a fireball at them.  Block the entrance to the doorway with your tank, then have your two-handed melee DPS do splash damage with a massive range and crit to wipe all the enemies out.  A bunch of the enemies are standing on a pool of water?  Not to worry--shoot an electrical charge at them and watch them all look like they dropped the toaster in the bath!  Surround the enemy leader, getting a flanking bonus, then Curse, Weaken, and Cripple him, set him on fire, and eliminate him from usefulness while his minions try and cut you down.  Fun for the whole family!
3.  Easy skill tree system.  Three skill levels (Novice, Adept, Master) and a point system which unlocks X number of each (so for example at Level 2 you can learn 3 Novice and 1 Adept).
4.  Object interaction is pretty ubiquitous and allows for fun strategies at times.  Cool and unique elemental magic/environmental effects.
5.  Fun world and mostly-cool storyline, when you get into it.  Please see my note below on voice acting as a caveat, however.
6.  Easy to use inventory system, UI is mostly fluid, and portal system is convenient.
7.  Vendors sell exciting gear with cool abilities and stats --- I had more fun buying gear than looting tbh.

[b] The bad --- [/b] 1.  Starts SLOW.  It's basically the Diablo 3 start --- quick and fun combat area (2-3 encounters) before town, but then once you're in town, you have to spend literally an hour picking up quests and clicking through dialogue which you do not care about at all yet.  There are literally 3-4 towns in the whole game, most of which are quick, and the first town takes a billion years to figure out wtf you should be doing.  Get past that and there's a great game waiting but I nearly uninstalled and asked for a refund.

2.  The voice acting is INCREDIBLY annoying.  All the actors oversell the pedantic and already-cheesy lines, and your heroes can't go 2 seconds without whipping off lame and wildly repetitive one liners.  For example every time they walk by a fire (which are everywhere) they'll say something like "I could use a cold drink".  However!  You can disable voice in Audio.  However!  This leads to losing all voice acting for potentially interesting plot scenes when they occur.  Personally?  I played it with Voice off as it was just way too annoying.

3.  Your characters sometimes disagree with your direction for no reason and then play rock-paper-scissors (literally) to see who wins.  If this doesn't sound frustrating enough, wait for it.  So, being a smart RPGer, you don't waste valuable attribute points on Charisma for both characters, right?  You pick one and optimise your other character for say, DPS.  Now, carelessly your non-charismatic character is active because he has Telekinesis and you are tired of walking to pick up all dat loot.  You engage in dialogue with an NPC.  Innocuous, right?  Until he says something like, "Should I execute my son for no reason? Mwah ha ha" and you're like "Uh no".  But then your charismatic character hops in and is like "The son deserves to die!".  Now because she out-charismas you, she auto-wins the argument, you execute the son and can't complete your quest, and then have to fight/murder the local townspeople who now think you're evil.  Sounds like fun, huh?  It's basically like doing a renovation with your mother--despite giving clear and logical instruction, you argue all the time and are forced to take irrational courses of action for no reason.

4.  Save often.  This game is mostly not that difficult but is very unforgiving and does not allow you to ressurect.  So for example you are cruising through every combat, and then one of your players does not call out a landmine and it blows up your whole party instantly.  Guess what?  Time to reload 15 minutes back.  No idea why they didn't just allow you to restart from where you were, it's standard practice and would have been so easy to implement.  Also it's very easy to accidentally kill NPCs who you need to not die (*casually clicks lever experimentally* *bombs inside prison blow up all the characters you are trying to free*).

5.  Mouse control is horrible to use.  Items are everywhere, and some of them move (e.g. trying to start a dialogue with a person, or worse, an animal, who tear around like madmen at all times).  Going through a puzzle area and accidentally click right next to something?  Woops your guy decided to jump in a lava pit setting off a cascade of bombs that kills your whole party.  I am a highly experienced gamer, this isn't just clickfailing or being bad: the problem is you left-click for everything including movement, speech, and looting...yes that includes stolen goods which means the whole town instantly attacks you.  This happens often and painfully.  See point #3 about not saving often and not auto-resing.

6.  Until you get a healer you need to portal to town every 2 mins to get to a bed.  The game is almost unplayable until you have a healer for this reason.

7.  Puzzle areas are very counterintuitive (which is pretty much the worst thing for a puzzle area to be!).  They're quite common and always bog you down with pointless and unchallenging but do-in-this-order style areas.  Also, forget one little UI intricacy like unchaining two party members, and one of them wanders along like an idiot walking into the landmine that blows everyone up.

8.  The stats & skills are poorly explained, especially the Abilities vs. Talents thing.  Most Talents sound super exciting when you get to level them at first--what, I can talk to animals or be a zombie?!  But then after you have 2-3 it turns out most of them are nearly (or utterly) useless or actually detrimental to take.

9.  Given how slow levelling is (max level seems to be 20), I keep feeling like the game is capped.  It's not a short game (I afk a ton so don't take my "Hours played" as in any way informative) but it feels like it will end at any moment at all times.  And yet given the slow build, really feels like an end game would be super enjoyable.

Once you get used to some of its painful parts, it's entertaining and immersive for hours (as long as you remember to save).  It's a great game but needlessly frustrating (to the point it feels almost trolly but it's too geeky to have been that evil).

I remember in 2002 when the Original Divinity game launched from Larian Studios.

Black Isle Studios / Troika Games produced some epic games such as Baldur's Gate, Fallout, Arcanum, Icewind Dale and Planescape Torment and on the wake of this success Larian launched this IP with Divine Divinity. The first game was buggy in places (and back in 2002 a bug required some ingenuity to get around because patches were difficult to come by) but it promised seriousness with a jagged humour. 

At this stage an avid young PC Gamer/RPG Fan like myself had no notion that this was going to be the peak of RPG Gaming for nearly two decades. Black Isle/Troika went to the wall and with them the promise of Baldur's Gate 3 and Fallout 3. Larian produced a second game in this series, in the form of Beyond Divinity. This had the same barbed humour and started as Divinity Original Sin 2 does which *SPOILER* sees the player behind bars. This became a bit of a trope (I strangely preferred starting a game in jail than washed up on a beach - looking at you Prince of Persia :P) and an effective one as it has been played out thousands of times in gaming history.

After this RPGs began to wane. Consoles became a more popular thing and the quality, detail and depth of RPGs started to become a thing from bygone eras as studios desperately aimed to cram as little as possible into a game so that it would fit onto a 700mb CD. Exceptions being the cadre of Final Fantasy Games - They just crammed in more CDS :p 

During this period it felt like many gaming studios struggled with their identity and/or just about keeping the lights on and I suspect Larian Studios was amongst these. In 2009 - 2010 Larian released Divinity 2 - an infinitely forgettable entry into the pantheon and in 2013 they released Dragon Commander which was an RTS and although it was based in the same universe and well received was a significant move away from the IPs roots. 

Then in 2014 Larian KICKSTARTED the IP again with this game - Divinity Original Sin. They captured the imagination of consumers by promising a game that held the quality, detail and depth that an RPG had at the turn of the century. They engaged with the community and developed what for me is one of the most mesmerising games since Baldur's Gate. This game is like a love letter to circa-2000 RPGs with its scripting, character development, freedom, twists, turns and frivolity. The game takes nothing seriously other than the craft of entertaining the player and Larian have created, in Divinity Original Sin, one of the finest examples of an RPG in history. It now feels like we may have entered another era where studios are producing RPGs of significant quality, detail and depth with Divinity Original Sin 1 + 2, Pillars of Eternity, Tides of Numenera, Wasteland 2 and Shadowrun. However, if history has taught me nothing it is that all good things will come to an end.

You owe it to yourself to buy and play this game and live its story. Good Luck and enjoy one of the finest RPGs in history before the sun sets on RPGs for another decade or three :)

Often overshadowed by it's predecessor and masterpiece (for good reason) Divinity: Original Sin 2, Divinity: Original Sin EE is still a fantastic product from Larian that started the Original Sin formula, and its something I highly suggest for anyone interested in checking out the Original Sin games, or if you are coming from Original Sin 2 (like I did) looking for another game like Original Sin 2.

The main thing I noticed with this game in comparison with its sequel is that its much more extreme and there's a lot more power curve. You'll find you start off (maybe a little too) weak and as you venture through the much brighter, more colourful world of Original Sin 1 Rivellon, you'll find it's definitely the same Rivellon you may have experienced before albeit it considerably more light-hearted and comedic. 

But its not before long when you figure out the formula of the game to be a lot more CC focused and you'll find elements are a lot more crucial to winning battles, it gives the player a lot more incentive to utilise elemental surfaces, grenades and consumables. (which I enjoyed far more than Original Sin 2) which makes for a nice change from 2, you'll start growing noticeably stronger as the game continues.

 In turn, (especially in the later game) this causes spells and abilities to feel a lot more impactful and capable of turning a battle around in a U-Turn, which isn't necessarily better than it's sequel but I definitely enjoyed it all the same, it just took me longer to reach this level and to actually understand what was possible with the spells.

Another great piece was the character interaction, due to the game having 2 characters from the beginning, they are already hard-programmed to compliment each other through interaction which makes it feel much more alive, entertaining and it introduces a very lovable duo to follow as the two of you have banter between each other as well as make decisions with a personality system that allows extra stats to be gained through agreement and disagreement with your cohort. Asides from this, the characters generally felt much more entertaining and fantasy, with a lot more quips and voicelines to accompany specific spells that are cast. Definitely one of the strengths over the lack of interaction between party members in Original Sin 2 

Though the game does possess technical limitations in comparison to 2, it can easily be excused as I am right to believe Larian was much more of an indie company during the development of this game, as they were co-developing Divinity: Dragon Commander alongside it as well.

You'll also find the story was definitely lacklustre, but it wasn't glaringly terrible and is still a good piece to accompany your characters journey through Rivellon.

All in all, I enjoyed the change up and though it was hard to start out with, once you establish your character you'll find yourself to be enjoying it a lot, and though it doesn't reward your imagination as much as 2 did (due to technical limitations, particularly with the teleport) it still rewards it plenty. I definitely recommend pushing through the early part of this game to enjoy the gem which is Original Sin EE, whether it be your first or second Original Sin game.

Phew. After a few hundred hours of playing this game I have finally beaten it as of this day. I love isometric RPG style games such as Pillars of Eternity, Divinity itself and even going back to the classic of Baldur's Gate. Divinity is unique in that it really stretches the bounds of what can be an ironically limited experience in the "infinity engine" style that isoRPGs tend to exist in.

I could not point out another game where I have read about a player beating the entire game on the hardest difficulty by throwing extremely heavy objects on top of enemies to crush them in one hit, using invisibility and telekinesis to slam their way through their battles not through strength of arm, not through prowess of mind, but through zany experimentation. That is, in essence, Divinity Original Sin. 

Divinity is a wild adventure of deep story, fascinating encounters, and unending freedom with how you take on the world as you go. The path is full of strange creatures, thoughtful characters, and many quests and storylines that make you wonder what was the right choice. Many times I had to stop and think for lengths on my choices, as they are not all straightforward problems with straightforward solutions. 

From unrestricted character creation, to an open world full of things to discover, characters with excellent dialogue, wonderful music by the late Kirill Pokrovsky, and a truly unique experience in what is a vast sea of games, Divinity is truly a divine experience.

However, that is not to say that this game is perfect. As much as I would like to end that there on a fanciful note, there are things (especially near the end of the game) that I noticed and did not enjoy or appreciate nearly as much as the rest of the game.

Exploration is part and parcel to the Divinity experience, puzzles, secrets, and all things in between are normal and expected along the way which it presents in itself from even the tutorial. However, that being said there are many times in this game that if not for guides or the internet at large, I would have never in my life have been able to continue this game. Things that I was stuck on until I finally gave up and searched, and where as the answers made sense, I couldn't fathom how someone actually figured that out. There are specific instances I could point to but I would rather leave this as spoiler free as I can. Again, where as I understand that Divinity is not just another RPG where you simply slam your head at enemies until you win the game, for me, the puzzles were sometimes so obtrusive and so expecting of what I feel was unbelievably complicated answers, that it hurt my own personal experience. But none the less, guides exist and you can access them nearly instantly unlike when we were young and needed to have guidebooks next to us.

Another negative point is that this game has places that feel incomplete, some threads that end in more questions than answers, and some big plot holes caused simply by how the game was built. There is an entire town that feels to have little purpose other than for one quest note before you ignore it and move on to somewhere else. Sure it has some shops but in an otherwise flowing and well charted world such things heavily stand out, and this did so extremely to me.

As for the previously mentioned plot holes, they exist in several ways. Whether it be that the players skipped a part of the questline but the game still acts like they did something, or the generic rpg problem of "we're scripted npcs so even though the problem is solved we're gonna talk about how bad things are still", or just things that don't really make sense but oh well it's 50 hours into the game i'm just gonna let it slide and press on. 

[spoiler]Also, in that same town aka Sacred Stone there is a prison, and if you did not outright combat the inhabits of the town (which are cultists in service of one of the leading antagonists) trying to free those prisoners is a NEGATIVE thing that will earn you NEGATIVE standing with the world. I believe this to be more a game creation "error" and overlooked in the grand scheme of the game. That being said however, there are no quests in that whole area, and it's only other purpose than another stop on the game's roadmap is for two of the companions questlines. You get the idea.[/spoiler]

Now the last thing i'm going to critic in the negative, beyond the puzzles, beyond the plot loops or weird endings, empty areas, intricate parts of the game I would have never understood otherwise. Is the finale of the game, beware this is heavy spoilers below.

Let me start by saying this: Divinity: Original Sin – Enhanced Edition is one of those games I didn’t expect to enjoy as much as I did. I picked it up because I heard good things about the combat and story, but I was unprepared for just how deep, smart, and genuinely fun this game is. It doesn’t try to be flashy or overly cinematic like some modern RPGs, and honestly, that’s part of its charm. It feels like a game made by people who love what they do, granting players a ton of freedom to experiment, solve problems in their own way, and enjoy a fantasy world that’s as weird as it is wonderful.

So yes, if you’re into strategy, storytelling, co-op play with friends, or simply exploring a rich world at your own pace, this game is definitely worth checking out. If you stick with me, I’ll explain why I think it’s such a great experience. 

[h1]First Things First: What Even Is This Game?[/h1]

Divinity: Original Sin – Enhanced Edition is a turn-based RPG developed by Larian Studios. The original version came out in 2014, and the Enhanced Edition followed a year later, featuring updated graphics, full voice acting, better controller support, and several quality-of-life improvements. You can play it solo or with a friend, which is great, and either way, you control two main characters who are Source Hunters—essentially magic cops trying to track down rogue magic users in the land of Rivellon.

At first glance, it looks somewhat old-school, featuring a top-down, isometric view reminiscent of classic games like Baldur’s Gate or Diablo. However, once you start playing, it becomes clear that this game is much more modern than it appears. It has depth, flexibility, a great sense of humor, and one of the best turn-based combat systems I’ve ever experienced in a fantasy RPG. 

[h1]The Story Is Cool, But You Get to Shape It[/h1]

The game begins with a relatively standard fantasy setup: investigate a murder in a coastal town called Cyseal. Sounds simple enough. But as you dig deeper into the story, it twists into all sorts of intriguing directions: time travel, ancient gods, cosmic balance, and alternate dimensions. It gets expansive, but in a good way.

What makes the story particularly enjoyable is how much control you have over it. You create your two main characters from scratch—not just their appearances and skills, but also their personalities and backstories. Throughout the game, these characters actually converse with each other, and you choose their responses. Do they agree all the time? Do they argue constantly? It’s up to you. These personality differences can impact how NPCs react to you and how some quests unfold. 

There’s also a lot of humor woven into the writing. This isn’t one of those grim, gritty RPGs where everyone is miserable. Sure, the stakes are high and there’s plenty of drama, but the game isn’t afraid to be weird or goofy. You’ll talk to animals, engage in arguments with sentient mushrooms, and solve puzzles involving teleportation pyramids. It never takes itself too seriously, and that balance works wonderfully.

[h1]Turn-Based Combat That Actually Makes You Think[/h1]

Now, let’s talk about the combat because this is probably the aspect that Divinity excels in. If you enjoy strategy games or tactical RPGs like XCOM, Fire Emblem, or Final Fantasy Tactics, you’ll likely love this. Every battle is turn-based, emphasizing positioning, elemental combos, and using the environment to your advantage. You don’t just spam attacks; you think about what surface your enemies are standing on (water, oil, ice), what spells you have, and how to chain effects together.

For example, you can cast -Rain- to soak the battlefield, then electrify the water to stun enemies. Or you might throw an oil barrel into a group and then ignite it with a fire spell for a massive explosion. There are so many creative combos, and experimenting is incredibly enjoyable. Sometimes things backfire—I’ve accidentally set my whole team on fire more than once—but even those moments add to the fun. 

Each character has a pool of action points (AP) that they spend to move, attack, cast spells, or use items. So every turn is like a mini chess match. Do you expend all your points attacking now, or save some for the next turn? Do you retreat to a better position, or try to finish off an enemy before they can heal? It’s tremendously satisfying when a plan comes together, especially in tougher battles. 

Regarding difficulty: Divinity can be challenging. Even on normal difficulty, you’ll encounter fights that punish careless play. However, the challenge is fair, and if you die, it’s usually due to a tactical mistake—not because the game is being unfair.

[h1]Customization and Character Building [/h1]

One of the aspects I adore most about Divinity is its flexibility. You’re not confined to a class system; you can build your characters however you wish. Want to be a tanky knight who also summons spiders and heals? Go for it! Or perhaps you want to dual-wield daggers and teleport around, stabbing enemies from behind? That’s totally possible. 

As your characters level up, you allocate points into various stats, skills, and abilities, with an extensive list to choose from. You’ll find standard fantasy abilities like Pyrokinetic (fire magic), Geomancer (earth magic), and Witchcraft (necromancy), as well as utility skills like Lockpicking, Bartering, and Sneaking. You can create a party focused solely on combat, or design quirky support builds that excel in dialogue, exploration, or puzzle-solving. 

And yes, the game is packed with puzzles. Some are straightforward environmental challenges, while others are complex brainteasers. You'll need to pay attention to clues, experiment with your tools, and think creatively.

[h1]Graphics, Sound, and Presentation[/h1]

Let’s be honest: Divinity isn’t the most graphically advanced game out there. It has a classic look—colorful and detailed, but not overly flashy. Nevertheless, it still looks great. The spell effects are satisfying, the character models are solid, and the environments are full of charm. 

The Enhanced Edition brought many graphical improvements, making everything feel smoother and more polished than the original. The user interface works well with both mouse and keyboard and controllers, and I never encountered any issues navigating the menus. 

The voice acting is another significant upgrade in the Enhanced Edition. Every line of dialogue is fully voiced now, and most of it is quite well done. This adds to the immersion, especially when interacting with quirky NPCs or unraveling complex quests.

And the music? Absolutely fantastic! The soundtrack ranges from chill, atmospheric tracks while exploring to epic themes during battles. I found myself humming a few of the songs after I stopped playing, which is always a good sign. 

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

Divinity: Original Sin – Enhanced Edition is one of those games that feels crafted with love. It doesn’t hold your hand, rush you, or try to be something it’s not. Instead, it offers a massive world, some of the best turn-based combat out there, and the opportunity to tell your own story in your own way. 

Whether you play solo or with a friend, it’s an experience that rewards curiosity, creativity, and patience. With all the enhancements in the Enhanced Edition—voice acting, controller support, and improved visuals—it’s the best version of the game to dive into. 

If you have even a slight interest in fantasy RPGs, strategy games, or co-op adventures, give it a try. It may take a few hours to really click, but once it does, you’ll be hooked.

This RPG has one of the best battle systems for a CRPG I’ve ever played, set in an interesting world full of exploration and memorable characters. It already starts strong with character creation  you can build your hero however you want, with no rigid class restrictions, which encourages experimentation right from the start. Then there’s the combat. It’s incredibly deep, systematic, and rewarding. The environmental interactions are brilliant. For example: cast a rain spell to soak the ground, then… Freeze it to create slippery ice (anyone who falls loses their turn), Electrify it to create a shocking damage field, or Ignite it to evaporate the water into steam that blocks vision (and yes, the steam can also be electrified). Or pour oil to slow enemies, then set it on fire to deal burning damage over time. Honestly, I often found the movement penalties more useful than raw damage this game taught me to value status effects and battlefield control as much as pure offense. That’s only scratching the surface; discovering different combos and team setups is half the fun. Crafting also ties naturally into gameplay like hammering nails into your boots so you don’t slip on ice (a surprisingly practical touch). 

You can min max stats if you want, but finding clever utility upgrades is far more satisfying. A heads-up you won't learn every skill in a tree, so a little planning or reading a guide helps. The world building and lore are excellent. I really enjoyed uncovering details about the setting and its side characters. The main plot is decent a bit familiar but still effective and your protagonists start mostly blank so you can shape them. Side quests, though, are where the writing shines motives feel believable, moral dilemmas hit hard, and the characters stick with you. You even assign personalities to your two main characters, and they will debate each other’s choices, adding flavour and sometimes influencing gameplay through a rock-paper-scissors-style system that gives small but meaningful stat boosts. The Tactical mode is a great extra challenge that doesn’t just crank enemy stats it reimagines encounters. Example (minor spoilers) the tutorial fight looks the same at first… until the first turn ends and you realize an extra enemy was hiding just off-camera, changing your whole approach. Later, I entered a battle near the first town and lightning kept striking, reviving electrified zombies that punished melee attacks. It’s clever, tense, and keeps you on your toes.

Overall, great game but deeply flawed and Original Sin 2 somehow manages to be even better.

Pros: 
1. Extremely satisfying RPG tactics combat that rewards logic and opportunism
2. Great class and ability system that lets you be creative with character builds

Cons:
1. Unreliable collision - 
Because the combat depends on measurements in 3D space, rather than a tile-based system or something like that, collision checks are precise and require precision on behalf of the user. However, the game doesn't facilitate this well.
Sometimes the game thinks your character is close enough to an enemy when they're not.
Sometimes your characters deftly navigate hazardous environments, other times they will get insta-gibbed by walking straight into lava.
Sometimes you'll have pixel-hunted for just the right spot on an enemy to target within range, only to have the camera move, or the character will animate, causing your click to do something completely different -- and there's no way to cancel or back out of an action.
What this means is that you'll never really trust the collision system to do what you want, and the kinds of mistakes that result from this system can be devastating, often being literally the deciding factor between victory and failure. Because the combat system is so well built on interacting mechanics, misfiring due to wonky control has unacceptable consequences.
I do believe this problem is highly solvable, but even in the Enhanced Edition, the problem is not solved.

2. Cryptic / Inconsistent Mission and Level Design
In most RPGs, if you're a little lost, you can just kinda explore and talk to people until you get yourself back on track.
Do not do that with Divinity. If you're stuck, just spare yourself the wasted hours and consult a spoiler-lite walkthrough or something. I have been off-track from missions for hours, and gotten myself way over-leveled due to just thinking I needed to explore more to find clear solutions. The game is not consistent about messaging how quests need to proceed, and the journal / log is nearly useless when figuring out what you're supposed to do next.
Worse, however, is many puzzles which depend on effectively pixel-hunting for tiny switches on walls.
I have a character with exceptional perception, and they will use that to call out cool secrets and hidden traps, which are helpfully highlighted. But when it comes to main-quest puzzle switches, this is of no help. You can hold down the ALT key to highlight items in the world, but switches will not show up.
All of this means that I stop being engrossed in the story anyway. I might as well just look up a walkthrough.

3. Turn-Based Except When It Isn't
Trying to use your characters' abilities outside of a combat scenario is needlessly annoying. Trying to use stealth, coordinate character movements to ambush enemies, using multiple spells from your different characters simultaneously... it's all useless outside of combat. If 2 of my guys catch on fire outside of turn-based combat, and 2 of them have healing spells, the burning damage will accrue on both in real time. However, if I start casting a healing spell on one, the other will have to wait for the spell to finish, while still taking the fire damage.
If you finish a combat encounter, the game kicks you back into realtime mode, which means you can't simultaneously heal up your guys who might still be under the effects of enemy spells. I have had characters die post-combat because of this.

Others:
The art, music and story are all serviceable. In my opinion the game depends far too much on its exhaustively lengthy writing, with helpful clues buried among walls of text that I tired of over the course of my 120-hour playthrough. While I may have some gripes about the scope, tone and pacing of the story, ultimately the killer is that the writing often felt disjointed from the quests I was doing. It became fluff that I was eager to ignore by the end.
The music is actually really good, but there's just not quite enough of it giving how hecking long the game is.

No complaints about the art, it does a good job selling a vibrant, if a little goofy, fantasy world. I'd prefer something that looks a little less like WoW proportions, and I don't like cyclops goblins and orcs with tails, but it's a matter of taste.
I would love to praise the game's co-op, but it's a feature that doesn't feel entirely useful in a turn-based game where I have to sit around and wait for my friend.

Summary:
So while I've complained a lot about the bad, I just want to say that this is easily one of the most satisfying RPGs with turn-based party combat I've ever played, and I'm very happy to have played it. The game is at its best when you're fighting, using your unique blend of abilities and items to solve combat just the way that suits your style as a player. It feels creative and fun in a way other turn-based party RPGs have never done for me.

It just sucks that there's so many questionable implementation choices that get in the way of that experience. If those problems are going to annoy you enough that good combat isn't going to make up for it, maybe give it a skip.
Here's hoping the sequel handles some of these things a little better (and Baldur's Gate 3 for that matter).

[h1]In-Depth Analysis[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
Narratively, DOS1:EE sits at the very top tier. From the beautifully animated, albeit rare hand-drawn cutscenes, conversations, banter, to the side lore found in books and documents, the writers have made sure each line of dialogue had its own distinct flair. Most of the characters you’ll meet will stick in your mind, not just plot-related ones, but almost all of them in fact. Despite there being hundreds, each of them has enough personality, quirks and mannerisms to result in someone you’ll remember, instead of the umpteenth generic NPC. The plot itself is articulate, interesting, and nuanced; it blends well the lines between good and evil, except for the final parts that, unfortunately, fall in the “insane villain” trope a bit too much. It’s ultimately a serious plot, that however doesn’t shy away from comedic, goofy tropes when appropriate, and never feels cringeworthy at any point in doing so.

The worldbuilding is deep and detailed, with much lore to be discovered in order to know more about Rivellon’s society, culture, issues and history. There sometimes are references to places and realms outside of it, but most of it is left to deduction or imagination; that’s not a bad thing, considering how much there already is to go through about Rivellon alone. All environments and locations have been made with the utmost care, subtle details and environmental elements adding an ulterior layer of depth to an already hefty lore package.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore on foot, with a handy map marking each important building and location once discovered, but covered by fog initially. Many locations, however, remain unmarked and will be up to you to place custom markers to remember them. A system of fast travel portals scattered throughout the land makes going back and forth convenient and immediate, while your personal Teleporter Pyramids, acquired very early, allow one character holding them to teleport to the other instantly. 

The Pyramids open up to endless exploration possibilities: throw them to use as beacons and cross gaps, put them into someone’s inventory with pickpocketing to access forbidden areas, use them to ambush your enemies, or as a retreat point if combat goes wrong. Barring a few areas inaccessible for lore reasons, exploration is non-linear and completely up to you; the only thing stopping you will be, mainly, enemies too strong to face yet. Other than that, there’re plenty of secrets (often found with high enough Perception, or knowledge from documents) and optional locations scattered throughout the four, large main locations, from dungeons to ruins and even dimensional portals. You never know what could be around the next corner, and DOS1:EE will surprise you time and again the more you delve into it.

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
Combat is turn-based, using AP for both movement, skills and other actions like using items or spell scrolls. The system is deep, with a plethora of status effects and elemental interactions to account for, other than the usual roster of resistances, weaknesses and stats like armor found in most other CRPGs. DOS1:EE however takes elements a step up from the crowd in how they interact: blood spilled on the ground can freeze and make anyone stepping on it slip, fire hitting water becomes steam, which can be in turn electrified to stun anyone nearby. Barrels of oil and poison explode when on fire, creating hazardous surfaces and smoke that blocks line of sight. These are just a couple of the many interactions you can use in combat to gain an advantage. But so will your enemies: the AI, especially for its time, is incredibly smart: enemies will give their back to walls if there’s a rogue around to not get backstabbed, use the elements in smart ways, and work with each other for coordinated actions.

Bosses are usually tough challenges, especially optional ones and those of your same level or above; they often possess unique abilities and talents. Great risks, great rewards: the system allows you to kill an enemy six levels above you, even if it’s almost impossible, and get enormous amounts of XP if you succeed. Given how much freedom of approach, items, and features you have to prepare for battle, it will be common to lay down traps, like barrel clusters or surfaces, before a fight begins to gain an advantage.

[h3]Character Progression & Roleplaying[/h3]
A standard XP-based system gives you attribute and ability points each level, and talents every few levels to further specialize each of your characters. XP is split in numbers, meaning a party of four will get less XP for each member than a party of two; you can’t play solo for lore reasons, but you can definitely have just two characters instead of four, even if that would mean missing out on the excellent companions’ writing and backstories. 

You won’t learn skills as you progress automatically; instead, skill books have to be found, bought or crafted in order to get new spells and abilities. The leveling system allows hybrid builds which allow more combat flexibility, and that can be just as effective, if not more so, than pure ones. The gameplay for each is markedly different, both in combat and outside of it, with activities like pickpocketing, charisma-related checks, crafting and trading taking a large chunk of what you’ll do when not exploring new areas.

Well. I can now confidently say that I have played through this game fully and I enjoyed most of it. In this game you get to gather party members and customize your party to your liking. No matter if you play this alone or with a friend, you get to discuss your decisions with your companions, AI and the other player as well. The turn based combat is amazing and intricate, making you plan every move to the T.

You play as a young Source Hunter, whose job is to rid the world of those who use the foulest of magics. The journey starts of as a simple murder investigation, but unravels to a worldwide disaster that affects the very fabric of time and space as well. It is up to you and your companions to save the world. This game really impressed me and kept me hooked till the very end. The story is really deep and immersive, even though there are parts that are very obvious and predictable. "Yet another basic Fantasy world" they say. Well yes, and? It has been expertly crafted, which is all we can ask for these days, as fantasy worlds pop up left and right. Rivellon is just original enough to make it interesting, even though it uses some common tropes within it's world.

The game play is very, very tactical, and some fights can last up to forty five minutes at times. Positioning, making sure you use potions and spells at the optimal moment, making sure you are well prepared for a fight; all of these points play a key role to success in this game. One single mistake can make you loose the battle and your companions. A lot of the game is based in dialogue as well; If you aren’t one for reading massive amounts of text (or listening to them), then you will probably want to avoid playing this game, as there is a butt load of text and dialogue to be found.

Graphics and visuals are absolutely fantastic! Lighting is so good and models and spell effects are fantastic. There are many areas in the game that are immersive and feel like they have been lovingly made, making sure every little detail looks good and immersive. The special effects are particularly gorgeous to look at and never get tiring. Sound effects and music is also usually great. Sure there's one or two tracks that aren't suitable, but almost all of it is pleasant to listen to and some are particularly lovely.

There was a few points that I wanted to bring up, that weren't all that great and kind of made me want to just stop playing. The dialogue choice disputes were very annoying when playing alone and were quite tedious. If an AI is set for a character, they will try to enforce decisions whenever they can. This is a problem because all disputes are settled with a game of rock-paper-scissors, which is ultimately a luck based game of choice. Sometimes the decisions were substantial enough that if the dispute was failed, I was forced to load a previous save, to get the choice I wanted. I learned quickly to save before dialogue when doing quests, so I was always prepared. 

Another point that was pretty useless to me was the crafting. Crafting was an unnecessary mechanic which resulted in my inventory getting filled up with crafting materials which require a lot of extra management. It felt like crafting was shoehorned in because it was popular at the time and it wasn't thought out completely.

Taking all of these points into consideration, I do think the game is very good and I would recommend it for sure. Just be ready for a lot of back and forth, and repeating and reading.

And now, [b]how to save hours of your life[/b](yes, literally hours) from inventory management hell:

[list]
    [*] Leather scraps are knife + leather (or just buy it)
    [*] Rope is yarn + yarn (definitely just buy it)
    [*] Backpack is leather scraps + rope
    [*] Make at least twenty backpacks
    [*] Give each character a backpack for each standard style of item
    [*] For example I have one for the char's equipment, one for healing, one for nades, etc...
    [*] Any special type of item(like keys) gets put in one backpack on one character
    [*] The backpacks are put on the 5th row of the character's hotbar, in the same order on each character
    [*] For example I have hotbar-1 as char equipment pack, hb-2 potions/food, hb-3 thrown damage, hb-4 scrolls
    [*] If a character is carrying a special item type then that pack gets put [i]after[/i] the standard types(example hb-9)
    [*] Sadly you can only have one pack open at a time, so...
    [*] To move an item you have to briefly put it into the characters main inventory, then where you want it end up
    [*] One character(preferably not the crafting one) is the buy/sell guy 
    [*] The buy/sell char's main inventory (stuff outside packs) is always and only stuff you're ready to sell
[/list]

The key is: backpacks can be put on your hotbar and never have to be manually accessed except for crafting.

There are some annoyances with this approach, foremost in my opinion being no autosort for the backpacks themselves, with a close second being you can only have one pack open at a time which can be a pain for your main crafting char. 
My solution was using the only unique looking backpack I've found(it's at the very start of the game) to hold all my misc crafting stuff. Then at the least I can always find that particular backpack easily.

But those are the basics! Obviously tweak it how you will, but I've played both with and without a solid inventory system.
Trust me. You need a system. It's like a playing a different game.

Which, aside from that, is a great game. 
Don't be afraid to branch out your chars a little to give them more utility. Even a single novice skill in another pool can take your character from 'ok' to 'ridiculously powerful'(looking at you, rogues).

I love crafting/blacksmithing in games(but not wasting stupid amounts of time) and these are the things I wish someone had told me before I started.

The 'original' Divinity Origin Sin was easily one of the best RPGs I had ever played. The game was mechanically one of the very few rpgs out there which stayed true to it's meaning. With the Enhanced Edition, the developers went back to their original masterpiece and cleaned up some of the rough areas which they really didn't have to do - yet they did and they did it for free.

The game has the classic good vs evil setup. One of things which I grew to love about this game is among the serious nature of the narrative, there is an equal measure of quirkiness which gave it it's own unique style.

The game is a CRPG at the core: Turn-based and a party of no more than 4 at a time. However, there is one aspect of the game which levitates the game among it's peers, the way how everything reacts with anything. Elements plays a huge part in the game and for it's part the game hands over complete control to the player (and enemies) on how elements behave with each other. For e.g. Calling in the rain brings water and makes everyone Wet. You can now zap them with electricity for a more powerful effects which stuns everyone foolish enough to stand over the puddle of water created from the rain. Or use the Wet status on your enemies and fire an ice spell to quickly turn them into ice. Once they are in ice form, they are more suspectible to Crushing Damage. You can then call in the fire to melt the ice to water, more fire will result in water vapor. If you you hit the vapor area with electricity, the vapor will turned into a crazy space of electric clouds, stunning anyone caught inside of it or stupid enough to get into it. The elemental system is one of the highlights of the game and can make the battlefield very unpredictable.

The Enhanced Edition of the game also introduces a full voice cast from top to bottom. The original edition only had a few voice options. I didn't expect the voice to be as good as they are in the newer edition. They also tweaked some parts of the game and completely reworked the ending for the better. So thank you Larian.

The game's greatest strength is how free-form the gameplay is. As a player as you gain knowledge on how the world reacts to every action, you are free to manipulate it as you wish. You can easily created situations which  the developers might have never intended for, yet it does not break the game, only makes it that much more interesting for the players to be as creative as possible.

I highly recommend this game. It is one of the most mechanically-perfect RPGs I've ever played.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]
Odd review time again, this game could be for you! There is so much right with it, it depends on if you can see through the flaws and embrace the virtues. 

So I finally played Divinity Original Sin: Enhanced Edition (DOS:EE). I’ve had this so long I didn’t even remember I’d been given a free copy of the EE. Thanks, devs, I really appreciate that. I was warned it was long… But I’m actually surprised it has more than a 10% finish rate… even the 7% finish rate of the original surprises me, it was a real slog. 

The easiest way to describe the gameplay, is that it’s [i]REALLY[/i] quite good… When you’re allowed. It’s a turn based combat system based around acquirable skills based on your class, with environmental modifiers. It’s very easy to learn, very satisfying to master and to cheese, and very poorly balanced if you’re under/over levelled. The problem, dear reader, is that [i]you’re not allowed to play unless you’ve done your homework.[/i]

But I’ll get into that in a little bit.

Much like every teenage boy on a message board post 2000, we are the source hunters. A dynamic duo who’s training, history, and entire lives are built around finding and destroying magic users wherever we find them. Naturally one of the first encounters in the game is with a shapeshifting magic user who we completely neglect to murder, closely followed by an encounter where we can recruit a mage to our cause in… hunting down and killing mages. 

Now before my propensity for being glib takes me, we should dive into the nuts and bolts. 


[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The music, voice acting, and general sound design is all delightfully nice. A lot will get repetitive if you spend the 80 hours with it that I did… But it doesn’t ever detract from the experience. 
[*] As previously mentioned, the combat system is fantastic. It can lead to some frustrations, however it is fundamentally well put together and extremely enjoyable. 
[*] The world is large, the maps are detailed, and you often get rewarded for exploration. This makes the hours you’ll spend combing the area for secrets much more bearable. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The biggest con, as previously eluded to, is that you simply aren’t allowed to play the game. 

i. Quests are supremely frustrating, with many taking multiple areas and a large swathe of time to solve. This could actually be a pro, however DOS:EE is terrible at explaining and choreographing. Sometimes you just missed a lever, sometimes you need to wait 12 hours to meet someone, sometimes you just didn’t hit the thing you’re meant to hit. There is very little hand holding, and that too could have been a pro. But there is also no intuitive way of knowing what to do or where to go. 

ii. Equipment is an excel spreadsheet of calculations. You need to reject an optimisation mind-set to truly enjoy this game. I could not. A [i]minimum[/i] of a third of my hours was spent comparing items and getting caught in an anxiety loop trying to determine which stats would be best, or searching every basket, bush, and rabbit hole for loot. Most of which I never used ‘in case I [i]need[/i] it later’. Sure you can argue that’s a user end problem, but I know you’d never put money down on me being the only one. 

iii. Another significant portion of my time was spent out of combat, waiting on healing cooldowns. Why? Because it’s a long walk back here, and it takes less time to wait minutes to get my puny heals to fill the hp bars. Sometimes I’d eat a ton of food, sometimes I’d use my precious pots… but generally, I needed to wait. And that’s not fun. 

[*] The game has such a poor inventory optimisation and gear distribution system. Give me one giant inventory and let me see everyone at once. PLEASE. Having to nip through each character to check everything every time drove me mental, to the point where my 4th character went into the final fight wearing crappy lvl 5 boots because that’s about the time I gave up on doing it all properly, and they were constantly being left out. 
[*] Another way the game grinds you to a halt is with the identification, charisma, and repair systems. These cost nothing but space in your inventory where you swap out clothes. It’s a bunch of added busy body steps and it’s a tiresome detraction from the fun parts of the game. It also adds to the anxiety when it comes to crafting and improving gear… but the bonuses improve with your level, so you’re forever lugging or storing stuff ‘to use later’ because it’ll be out of date in 5 minutes when you can make a better one or you’ll find something even better than that stuffed up the arse of a nearby goblin. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Single inventory with all characters on screen to do gear.
[*] Restrict loot to prevent this comparison nightmare – it wouldn’t be a problem if it were just one character, it’s because there are 4 it’s an issue. 
[*] Consume keys on use, don’t give us stupid inert stones, use up quest scrolls if they’re never going to be used again, give us an indication on if we’ve read a skill/passive book. Make it open or something. This would reduce the busy work even more.

Usually, I give games a fair chance, but Divinity is a game which didn't hold my interest at first. I only put a few hours into the game and gave it a 'meh' review. I recently got hooked on its sequel, Divinity 2, and decided to give the first one the fair chance it deserved.

I'm happy that I have. It's an amazing game, with a memorable soundtrack and combat that really feels better than I gave it credit for. I originally thought skill books were going to be a rare commodity, but it turns out they're readily sold at various merchants in town. Oops.

The game is even better with a friend, which causes you to either work together or butt heads to accomplish your goals, occasionally (or often) entering disputes as to what the right choice is. The desputes are handled in game as well through a game of paper rock scissors. It's actually more clever than I gave it credit for originally, and while it does leave persuasion attempts up to chance, really it's no different than dice in that respect. You just enter a furious dramatic paper rock scissors game with the person you're trying to persuade (with advantage or disadvantage depending on your skill).

Honestly I highly encourage anyone interested in trying this game to play it with a friend, as the experience is a lot richer that way. Though the game itself is still easy to appreciate when solo. I originally shut it out due to how 'old school' it was, but when I gave it another try it warmed up to me emmensely.

The combat is turn based and complex. A battle can be won using a variety of tactics, to include creating and manipulating elemental surfaces such as water, fire, oil, and the like. If you don't have the means to create a desired surface there are barrels aplenty full of dangerous substances  ready to sustain your abuse. Come to think of it, why do these barrels exist? Why are there barrels of poison just laying around? Eh, who cares, they're pretty darn useful.
