[h3]Divinity: Original Sin - A Reborn RPG Classic[/h3]

Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition is a reimagined version of Larian Studios' acclaimed RPG, blending the soul of classic CRPGs with modern systems. This isn't just a remaster: it's a refined, deeper, fully voice-acted RPG where every choice matters, and every battle demands tactics.

[h3]Two Heroes - One Fate[/h3]

You control two Source Hunters - tasked with rooting out a dangerous magic that threatens the realm. Together, they're pulled into a conspiracy that could upend the world. The game shines in its cooperative mode (split-screen or online), where players can argue, cooperate, or betray - all of which affect the story.

[h3]Tactical Combat Without Mercy[/h3]

The turn-based combat is a true gem. You combine elements, set traps, and use the environment: fire ignites oil, water conducts electricity, and poison can be blown up. Every battle is like a fantasy-flavored chess match.

[h3]A World That Plays by Its Own Rules[/h3]

Rivellon isn't just a backdrop. Everything is interactive: you can steal, pick locks, talk to animals, or find hidden stashes. The story is non-linear with dozens of side quests, and nearly everything can be solved in multiple ways - from diplomacy to mass destruction.

[h3]Voice Acting, Humor, and Atmosphere[/h3]

The Enhanced Edition adds full voice acting, an improved interface, new skills, and a reworked ending. Dialogues are rich with Larian's signature humor, and moral dilemmas rarely have a "right" answer - only consequences.

[h3]Verdict: For Thinkers, Explorers, and Replayers[/h3]

Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition is a perfect choice for fans of hardcore RPGs. It's a game you'll want to return to, trying new builds and different choices. Best enjoyed with a friend - someone you can argue with over every decision.

My first Larian game was Divinity Original Sin 2. I thought it was absolutely fantastic and so I bought Baldurs Gate 3 the day it left early access. It went on to become one of my favourite games of all time and I needed more. Rather than wait for Larian to put out a new game, I decided to give their back catalogue a chance. Divinity: Original Sin Enhanced Edition may be older and lacking in production values, but it was still a fantastic experience that really felt like a Larian game. Like all of the Larian CRPGs I have played, not only is it fully voice acted, but the voice acting is fantastic.

The game has you create 2 characters and then throughout the first act allows you to recruit 2 additional companions. You play as source hunters, essential the magic police, who are sent to investigate a magical murder. This is done both by talking to people and fighting enemies in a turn based combat system. Like all Larian games, the combat is really great and it was neat to see a persuasion system that doesn’t just rely on a simple skill check, although this does mean you can quick save and reload to guarantee a win if you so choose. Overall I don’t think my dialog choices mattered all that much, which was a bit disappointing, but I enjoyed the game more than enough to make that a non issue for me.

Of course the game is missing some QOL features of newer Larian games, but it is much less than I was expecting. The biggest annoyance I have is how slow healing is. I have a healer in my party and I understand why they cannot spam their healing spell during battles, but making me wait 30 seconds between healing each character after every battle does get a bit annoying, especially when I cannot control any of my characters or view their inventories for the first 5 or so seconds after casting the spell. Additionally, I thought that several of the puzzles was not well designed. There were a handful of times that I had to give up and google the solution, only to find something I’m not sure how anyone would have solved without spending literal hours trying hundreds of completely random things.

There was also some wired bugs, like teleportation spells not working in most areas, or attacking an enemy resulting in my charterer walking towards the enemy instead of attacking them like the UI indicated would happen. There was also a small handful of random dialog that had no voice acting, even though the sentence before and after had voice acting. Nothing that I would consider super major, but thees issues were a bit annoying to deal with.

Overall Divinity: Original Sin Enhanced Edition is a fantastic experience. While it may be shorter, taking me only 65 hours to beat, I actually think I may have enjoyed it more than Divinity: Original Sin 2. However, that very likely is recency bias since it has been a number of years since I played the sequel, and I will fully admit my memory of it is quite foggy. This game definitely is not be as good as Baldur’s Gate 3, but it’s also about a decade older and still holds up very well. You can totally see how this turned into Baldur’s Gate 3 and for anyone who played that and wants more or is interested but cannot afford it, I would highly, highly recommend this game.

Divinity: Original Sin is what Larian studio needed to create to reach the level of polish and quality that is presented in D:OS2. This review is coming from someone who played through the sequel first, so if you are in the same boat, then my experience is relevant to you.

[h3] Story [/h3]
(Minor spoiler warning) The game is set in Rivellon before the events of D:OS2. This time you are playing as the hunter, rather than the hunted. In certain aspects the formula is the same. You get thrown into a mess in the beginning and gotta talk to a bunch of people, then realize you are involved in something big, then plot-twist and twist and tada you save the world. However, the delivery is rather predictable and cliche, so don't expect anything mind blowing. The side characters are interesting enough to tag along and the whole setting is engaging enough to keep going til the [spoiler] rather anti-climatic [/spoiler] end.

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]
This is where the weakness of the game starts to show. There is no terrain advantage which makes positioning a lot simpler here. Ranged characters often get blocked by invisible barriers around objects. Action point cost for certain setups like dual wielding is too punishing, while it can be very favorable to a ranged glass cannon. Some high-end skills would make more sense as a lower-tier one (e.g. swap characters) and vice versa.

Skill upgrade costs are cumulative, which means you need to invest 5 skill point to get something to level 5. While the game does a good job of balancing it out, it is just unnecessarily complicated. Meanwhile, upgrading some skills like loremaster are completely pointless since you can always identify items with traders and you get enough money from just selling your loot.

Resetting the character is only possible after circa. level 10 and you lose all the skills you have learned if you choose to do so, and you'd need to gather books and relearn them. By the way, there is no memory mechanic and you can use all the skills you have learned. There is just a limit on total skills you have based on your level, e.g. at level 5 pyro you can have 10 different pyro skills. From upgrading a skill to the last level all you get is an additional master skill slot, which is quite underwhelming considering most master skills can be used only once per combat.

I could go on and on, but that should give you an idea that if you have seen the second, you will be annoyed with the first.

[h3] Classic RPG or Chore RPG?[/h3]
Don't get me wrong, I like hearing NPCs talk about their life and learn the lore bit by bit from a lot of conversations and books. There are a lot of interesting side-quests that are not black and white and face you with some thought provoking decisions. But sometimes you are faced with a quest in the beginning of the game that can only be wrapped up much later in the game. Sometimes, you try to talk to every NPC, read every book, and look everywhere but still the next step is not clear. I even had some quests break and become impossible to complete because I did not talk to a certain NPC before exploring. I often found myself looking at guides and wikis, specially in the end when I realized some of the clues are impossible to pick up on during gameplay. [spoiler] Like I have to light some torches for a magic door to open in a cave? what? [/spoiler].

[h3]Worth a try[/h3]
In the end, it is more divinity if you have not been able to scratch that itch after playing D:OS2. While it lacks a lot of the good features introduced in the sequel, it still stands above most competitors. Give it a shot, and if you start to get frustrated with not knowing what to do, look up a guide.

Olympus with its phenomenal engineered throw back to the old school era of RPGs, but with its own, unique, "new school flavor"; all wrapped in a pretty bow - as in the interactable world and environment built around it. Dvinity plays just like the "oldies, but goodies", yet with a refreshing approach implementing new elements to modernize the dead genre while breathing new life into the RPG's of old. 

Despite bridging the gaps by filling in the missing components of the early century Golden Age of "bird's eye view RPG's", Divinity reaches beyond the limitations of the earler "industry defining" releases in the open world RPG genre. Divinity offers an unpredented depth to character development by offering a plethora of archtypes, styles of play, and even so far as each character's personality through an AI setting to be available at release. The "AI" setting is your characters disposition, which I look forward to experiencing the impact it will have with NPC interactions, and the game play as a whole. Divinity makes the world around the player character come alive and cooexist with the player character's choices offering a synergy unlike what you have seen before in an open world, "choose your own adventure", RPG's.

Combat is of course turn based, and strategic to say the least; in many situations, survival is contingent on casting spells on the environment for special bonuses and effects against your combatants. Spells, certain weaponry - particularly arrows bought or crafted by Rangers - as well as skillsets also help the player navigate and negotiate dangerous environmental restrictions such as, poisonous areas, grounds scorched by fire, or frozen over by ice, and environmentally hastened, strengthened, and even weakened, enemies. Only by negating or taking advantage of these effects can your characters safely gain passage whether they are navigating through dangerous environments, or fighting certain combatants requiring the player to use thought and purpose to progress through the game.

You start with two fully customizable characters based on existing archetypes, or you can build their skill sets and spell pools to your own style of gameplay. During your travels you will be introduced to other companions who will join your crusade with their own personal disposition towards your actions and inactions with ongoing interactions with your player characters as the game progresses. Your chacters themselves will also interact through dialogue to support one another's choices or to contradict eachother using skills gained during gameplay through these interactions and their AI plays a role in their decisions.  Will they support your actions, take opposition, or will it lead them to despise everything about you and what you stand for as a person?

Divinity offers a deeply rich environment. The backstory is that the player characters are "Source Hunters", or investigators that quell threats of people using an evil form of necromancy magic called, the "Source". It all begins with the investigation into a murder at Cyseal, requiring the player character to interact with several NPC's to unravel the mystery until their investigation leads to fruition with answers to satisfy the residents of Cyseal. 

Quests, in general, are multilayered requring the player to embrace and comtemplate their interactions with NPCs as they progress through the story of unravelling the mysteries to find the answers their quest-givers seek. These quests are not at arms length or fetch quests. Rather the quests contribute to the finality of the game and your cause as the protagonist. Most of them, even the side quests, represent a link in the chain of steps to achieve your ultimate goal of completing the game. This provides a sense of unity and singular purpose in discovering the solutions whereby what you decide to do in one quest may ultimately affect the results of another or multiple quest chains. This offers a very unique experience to RPG players both old and new. Players generally have to interact with most of the NPCs in order to decipher what needs to be done to complete each quest, while certain quests still maintain a simple and direct passage offering diversity. Once you have completed the quests in one area, they transition to the next area, and so on and so forth until you reach the finality of the game as the protagonist. Notwithstanding the many stages, quests feels organic and intuitive and whether they are substantive or minute, you feel a sense of accomplishment as you tally forth into the unknown.

To advance the experience further, Divinity includes crafting similar in scope and application from genre defining games like the Ultima series. You can craft an innumerable number of items, from clothing to weapons, potions to scrolls, magic items to non-magical items, all based on your crafting skills, the necessary components, the recipe books you have uncovered, and through the simple function of trial and error by mixing various ingredients to discover new compounds. The crafting component offers an entirely additional layer and value to the game that can keep you entertained for hours, if only to learn more combinations to create items, potions, weapons, and then twice over by mixing crafted items with crafted maigcal items to create magical properties within crafted items.

Divinity: Original Sin is truly the RPG borne from and infused with old school RPG DNA. If you are a purist when it comes to isometric RPG's, you will not be disappointed with the depth, novelty, and versatility of this game. Not only does the game offer a core storyline for you to playthrough, but additional tools to afford players to create their own environments, NPCs, characters and quests to upload to developer servers for others to play. These tools offer the level of depth that most online games with similar tools could only dream of providing to their player base.

You would probably expect that I would be wrapping up this review, but there's more. The game can be played single player. One of the more defining characteristics of this game is the opportunity to have one player character controlled by a second person. You can play with a friend and divide and conquer, performing whatever actions you choose free from the other player and all across the environment.

Your decisions do not weigh lightly in this game, but rather define the your experience through to the finality as well as how the world may interpret your actions for the better and for the worse. This is worth every cent if you are an RPG lover, and Divinity truly sets a new precedent and the bar high for all RPG titles released after its full publication.  The next iteration of this game will be released in the last quarter of 2016, so if isometric turn based RPGs shares a special place in your heart, buy the game now and lead your way into the sequel that is expected to be released later this year.

[h1]Rating: awesome (9/10)[/h1]

[b] Introduction [/b]
Divinity: Original Sin is an immersive RPG with a long main story quest line, great amount of non-generic side quests, well written dialogues and beautiful graphics. The gameplay is perfectly designed for a fun co-op experience, which combined with humorous dialogs that players encounter, and turn-based combat system create a mix that sets a new milestone in coop interaction.

🔵 PROs 🔵[list]
[*] Game is designed to be played in co-op with 2 players (moddable to 4 players on own risk)
[*] Great combat system with a lot of interaction between the players
[*] High amount of spells and abilities which you can combo into new effects
[*] Immersive storyline and non-generic side quests
[*] Funny dialogues and situations
[*] Amazing voice overs, soundtrack and overall musical compartment
[/list]
🔴 CONs 🔴[list]
[*] Some quest decisions may change your character stats in an unwanted or unexpected way
[*] Balance of different spells and attacks in the base game is a bit off-set (fixable with mods)
[*] Lots and lots and lots of random chances on your attacks, spells and saving throws
[/list]

*NOTICE* I will be rating the base game provided by the developers of Larion Studios, however for the full experience of this game I suggest downloading and installing the "Epic Encounters" mod, which greatly enhances the game. It adds new quality content, changes the balance of spells and abilities as well as increases the difficulty for more insane and cool fights.

[h1] Gameplay & Story: 9/10 [/h1]
Source is a special magical energy which was banned from the land of Rivellon ages ago, but recent events showed that there is a new secret organisation using it for their dark purposes. Players, which control two Source Hunters, an organisation that is focused on getting the land rid of all the Source are sent on a mission to investigate a murder where supposedly Source was involved. The journey beginning in a city of Cyseal takes players through a great amount of different locations, ranging from deep forests to ice covered land of fairies. The murder case of course unravels as a part of a bigger scheme, which however is not a simple linear and obvious case.

[h1] Combat & Challenge : 9/10 [/h1]
Turn based combat, which in tactician difficulties combined with the Epic Encounters mod provides quite a challenge. Since the magic schools are based on elements lot of spells are the classical known fireballs, ice shards, meteor rain etc., but there is quite a great amount of spells, which provide either unique interactions or certain effects which can be combined for a greater impact. Enemy types range from typical undead zombies immune to poison and sturdy green powerhouses called orcs to demons and elementals. Most of the boss battles contain some kind of mechanics to spice up simple tank & spank which can be used on most common opponents. Best part of the combat is the interaction possible between the characters, for example one creating an oil surface with earth magic, while the second lighting it up with fire spells or grenades. It is possible to recruit up to two more companions, which provide their own unique sets of abilities and can be developed in almost the same way as the main characters.

[h1] Graphic & Interface : 8/10 [/h1]
Divinity:OS not only contains a great story and amazing immersion level, but also provides detailed graphic design which was noticeably hand-crafted in a lot of places visited throughout the game. There is a range of different settings inside the areas and each has a different unique touch, be it weather, ground elements which can be used in combat or traps. Beautiful story parts are shown in hand-crafted art when the player starts to unravel the story of Rivellon. All the gear found directly changes the looks of your character in the game world. The interface is simple, yet has detailed information about all the needed mechanics, traits and attributes. It fits the art style while not clunking up the screen as in a lot of other RPGs.

[h1] Progress & Mini-Games : 8/10 [/h1]
The progress in Divinity:OS is pyramid styled - the player receives a great amount of quests shortly into the game, some of which are actually unfinishable at this point of the game, with a steady decrease towards the end of the area. Once a new area is started, another batch of quests can be accepted in a new town. Lot of the quests though have different endings based on the protagonist’s decisions and can even have an impact on the characters! Some quest lines can be finished quite already with an easy and direct solution, however if the needed time is taken to uncover the truth behind the story, it may lead to a completely different decision and ending of the quest line, resulting also in other rewards and possibly even world changes. As for mini-games, there is a classical "rock, scissors, paper" mechanic implemented, if the players do not agree on a certain set of actions when facing a decision in a situation or quest resolution.

[h1] Audio & Immersion : 9/10 [/h1]
Not many words have to be spoken about the terrific music and over all sound design in this masterpiece, because even after 250 hours into the game, I have not turned the music or the sound off and still continue to play with the great sound accompaniment Larion Studio provided us.

[b] Side-Notes [/b]
[list]
[*] Divinity:OS offers a long co-op player campaign and a great amount of non-linear side quests.
[*] This game contains steam trading cards which are easy to achieve.
[*] It contains steam achievements, most of which are easy to unlock with normal gameplay, however some may require replaying the game with different decisions.
[*] DOS offers major replay ability, in which players can decide to partner with other companions, solve quest lines differently or try to finish other steam achievements.
[/list]

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Divinity: Original Sin is an overall awesome game which laid new milestones in co-op gaming development providing new and unique ways of player interaction, cool combat design with spell and attack combo system, which builds heavily upon player interaction. An immersive campaign with well-written dialogs and quest stories, which continues throughout the whole game and is not spliced into different unconnected chapters is a rarity to find in games these days. Everything in Divinity shouts that a lot of love went into the details, atmosphere, background as well as main mechanics, that even non-gamers will most likely get their dose of fun and enjoyment from this game. After finishing this game for the third time (this time with my non-gamer girlfriend), we are both hyped for the 2nd part of Divinity: Original Sin.


I hope this review helps you making the decision if it’s worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

By far the new standard in Couch Co-op games.

No longer is  Player 2 invisibly bound to Player 1 by some kind of autoscrolling window game of running man simulator.

Quest, loot, fight, flee, craft, and create your own experinces independently, with a dynamic same/split screen interface. 

Divide your party and combine again at any time through useful tools, like; Synced log/quest book, synced crafting recipies, magic pockets, send to player inventory, shared map/quest markers, and warp to player. 

Use the character classes for Co-op role play, with skills like leadership for example granting bonus's to the characters when they are together.

Disagree with your flat-mate on whether or not those guards should be killed for treachery? Don't like how your girlfriends Cleric has decided to end a conflict peacefully?   Oppose them in dialogue and force the issue to the fate of virtual rock, paper, scissors.   Win and the desicion is made, lose and have comfort that your characters personality is still affected by your protest.

If your party is not prepared for combat, they will easily get wiped out.  The combat is difficult because your party is out numbered and out levelled in most situations.  There are only a finite numbers of enemies on the map so you cannot “grind” to level your party up or get better loot.  The game is laid out in a linear way which forces your party to outsmart your enemies by using the proper spells and environment surroundings.

I can appreciate the work done by this indie game developer, but I find this game is little too hardcore for my taste.

It was made especially worse by having my voice volume still on, hearing all of the merchants shout the same repetative lines about their wares over and over with very little respite.  

I had to eventually turn the voices off, and while it certainly made going about the town a little easier I still would've liked to have seen the ammount of things to do there broken up a little bit.  As a video game player who wants to explore every inch of a location before leaving, the value of everything I was learning felt lessened because of how much there was to see in the town. I *hated* learning about the "End of Time" and the true mystery behind the game.  To avoid specifics as much as I can, i'll simply say that a plot-line based around you being the 'fated hero' who is the only possible one who can save the universe was the true travesty the game committed (especially when it happens so fricken' early on!).  

I was sold on the idea of being a Source Hunter running around cleaning up magic hoo-hah and making the world a better place or whatever. "Found another star stone?  Well go back to the End of Time!", "Major plot-point just occured?  Better go back to the hub and talk about it with your pals!"  Gah!  No!   ...I eventually stopped playing, just before the end of the game, my enthusiasm having fully been eroded away.  As a person who loves stories and with that being such an important part of this game, I cannot recommend this one.  Hopefully Divinity Original Sin 2 will do better in this respect.

You know how it's common for people to say "I wish there was a 'mixed' option" for steam reviews? Well, I'm gonna go one step further. I wish there was a 'null' option for steam reviews, as in--I neither reccomend nor wish to stray people away from Divinity.

Because, as I sit here, two steps before the end of the game, I realize that I cannot in good faith reccomend this game to anyone, regardless of their preferences. I very firmly believe that no one could ever make it to the end of Divinity and seriously believe it is a great game. It has so many absolutely unbeliveable flaws--that were apparently never fixed or even got [i]worse[/i] in this allegedly "Enhanced" edition. But the perverse irony is that I actually did enjoy Divinity. Quite a lot actually. I can safely say that I will [i]never[/i] play this game in singleplayer again, but I somehow stepped away from the astonishing mess that is Divinity and came out with a positive experience. Put through rigorously systemic analysis, Divinity is a terrible game, but is a terrible game that I somehow ended up enjoying more than almost every RPG I've played in the past 5 years.

The strength of Divinity, as you'll read in every single positive review, is the combat. It is [i]very, very good[/i]. The encounter design, especially during the beginning of the game, is beyond excellent, with enemies (in hard mode) placed in positions that are advantageous for you but appropriate for them, and they usually outnumber you, so you have to use crowd control wisely. Thankfully crowd control is not restricted only to magic classes as it is in other fantasy RPGs, as not only can a warrior-type very easily choose to learn basic crowd-control magic with no fuss, but there are grenades that function as throwable spells. Everything is so well balanced while never feeling homogynous--Fighters get many knockdown effects, Rogues get area control and invisibility, etc. What impressed me most is the difficulty curve, or rather, the linearity of it--almost every fight is decently challenging (on hard mode) as long as you stay within the same levels as your enemies, and yet none of it ever feels excessive, there's no moment where I was ever saying "How am I expected to do this?" because the game makes your options very clear to you. There *are* a few moments towards the end of the game where your super-powered level 20s can effectively end even supposedly difficult encounters in a single round, but by that point the game is pretty much over.

So what are these "unforgivable flaws"? I'll make this simple and list them:

[h1]It's Time To Stop[/h1]

Divinity is way, way, too long, and the pacing is [b]horrendous[/b]. Divinity has a serious problem where playing for short periods of time will lead to you making no concievable progress whatsoever, and playing for a long period of time will put you through so much work and combat that it will turn into an unmemorable grind, which is not only bad in and of itself, but also unproductive towards finishing the game because Divinity's quests really do want to make sure you have things memorized and understood. 

So much in Divinity leads towards this feeling of endless grind, to the point where I can't even indicate one specific thing as the culprit. One of the biggest problems is that there is too much combat, but it's not only that there's too much combat, it's that the combats themselves are [i]very[/i] long and beyond about 50% of the game, many of them are complete repeats of fights you've already done. Then there's the puzzles, the constant save-scumming trap rooms, pixel-hunting puzzles, incredibly long quests with no sense of direction, it just goes on and on.

The scope of the game, both narratively and mechanically, is stretched out as far as it can go. Many RPGs have the classic "Level 1-20" system just because D&D did it, but they won't be insane enough to actually put all 20 levels of difficulty into one game. Not Divinity. You'll immediately start out fighting hordes of slow-but-powerful undead, but in the middle of the game you'll be fighting elementals that can inflict every status imaginable on you, to the point where, by the end of the game, you are fighting enemies that are [i]literally invulnerable[/i] for a few rounds at a time. 

The most absurd part is that it doesn't even tether enemies to conventional expectations of their levels. You don't fight wolves until level 7. You don't fight goblins until you're level freaking 12. One of the most difficult encounters in the entire game is against a horde of spiders at level 14. So of course they get new, nonsensical abilities appropriate for that level. This leads to insanity like an alpha wolf casting a Mass Disease spell, or a zombie drinking a healing potion. Giant crabs can fucking deal Attribute damage to you--in an AOE. It's a bizzaro world.  You know that old image where the caption says "There was a point where we needed to stop and we have clearly passed it--but let’s keep going and see what happens"? That's Divinity encapsulated.

[h1]Traps and Perception[/h1]

Divinity has traps. Divinity has traps everywhere. Divinity has traps everywhere that are invisible to the naked eye and can kill your entire party if you step on one. So how do you deal with these traps? Well, basically, you don't. There's an Attribute called Perception which grants a slight amount of AP to your first action in combat but otherwise does nothing (not even an acccuracy bonus) except allow you to detect hidden secrets and traps. The way this works is that there's a hidden value for each trap and secret in the game, and you need that much perception to see it. This is dumb enough by itself--Perception is essentially a tax that one of your characters has to pay to even be able to play the game. It's a "you must be this tall to ride" sign, codified as an attribute. Dumb.

But the icing on the cake is that even [i]with[/i] Perception, you can't really do jack shit about traps. The radius in which you can detect traps with a high Perception character is often lower than the effect radius of the trap itself. Therefore the only way you can detect traps is to actually set them off, i.e., get yourself killed. Then you reload (because you WILL be quicksaving every other second in this game, or you WILL lose massive amounts of progress), and either throw a combustion spell over the trap or summon a minion on top of it. To add insult to injury, most of the time your summons can detect things better than your high character. Not that it matters, because even if you have the insane luck to spot a trap before it activates, you still need to disarm it, for which you need to use a consumable item, or shoot it. 

[h1]Rock Paper Reload[/h1]

In Divinity, there are actually two protagonists. If you play multiplayer, each of you gets to make your own hero. If you play single player, you get to make two heroes, and while you control both, you only control one for each conversation. In 2P, there are points during conversation where the player who is not instigating conversation gets to chime in. In 1P this happens as well, but with an AI controlling the result instead. For some reason, the AI will almost always choose to disagree with every choice you make, which is bad enough by itself. But what's even worse is that the AI can actually [i]override[/i] your choices. If you disagree, you have to play RPS with them. Literally. 

Whoever wins, wins the "argument" and makes the choice. This means that not only does every single choice force you to play a minigame, but you may not even get to make the choice you wanted to make. The worst part of this is that it can be completely avoided by savescumming; effectively the developers accomplished nothing but wasting the player's time.

So why did I eventually choose to click thumbs up rather than thumbs down? Because honestly, I think this game needs to be played. People need to know just how utterly insane it is.

This game is amazing. The story is fantastic. The gameplay is fun, BUT I would never recommend this game. The game design in Act 2 and prior to the conclusion is so BAD and so BROKEN that it genuinely sucks the soul out of you. I'm convinced 90% of these reviewers have forgotten what it's like to play this game for the first time not knowing where to go. 

Act 2 is lvl based areas in a full circle and it does not do a great job of guiding you in the right direction. I managed to get halfway through 3-4 quests before getting lvl capped and absolutely destroyed by enemies before stumbling into the right areas. It ruined my immersion and sent the story into a confusing spiral for me. 

Throughout the game you collect Star Stones. What the game doesn't tell you is you are required to get them all to progress to the final fight. I'll finish the game, but currently Ive spent 3ish hours aimlessly wandering the map and searching forums trying to figure out which stones I've grabbed and which ones I've missed, because the game doesn't have a system to keep track of that for you. As I said, terrible design. 

It pains me to give this a negative review as I have loved the 60+ hours I've thrown into it, but the flaws are too big to overlook.

I came back to this game because of the steam deck, it runs exceptionally well on it! The game clearly didn’t have the same budget af DOS2 and BG3, and this mainly shows in the poorly designed puzzles and relatively shallow story. But if you don’t mind looking up the solution to a puzzle now and then, and don’t mind shallow NPCs, then the game can be pretty fun. It has solid combat mechanics, a lot of decent voice acting, and good character customization options.

Admittedly, this game took me a while to get into— surprising, considering that Divinity: Original Sin 2 is my favorite game. I bounced off this entry three or four times before finally knuckling down and sticking with it, and I'm very glad I have. I've spent years looking for a game that plays anything like D:OS2, and, of course, it's this. I just had to get past Cyseal to see how much it shines.

The first few hours of the game were super confusing to me. Every time I felt sure that I knew where to go and what to do, my party was far too miserably under-leveled to even attempt it, so I ended up looking up guides a lot, and I'm genuinely impressed by anyone who has finished this game without one— some of the quest lines are incredibly convoluted. Still, I'm having a blast playing now. I can see all the mechanics that were polished and brought over to D:OS2, and it makes me appreciate that much more just how incredible the second entry is while still enjoying the first.

I'm just about finished with the Luculla Forest map, so I'm guessing I'm getting somewhat near the end. The story is interesting, the combat is fun, and the voice acting is delightful (hearing so many familiar voices doing an assortment of accents and changing up inflection to sound like different characters is fantastic— especially when they're sitting right next to each other in game, chattering away with the same voice). I still prefer D:OS2, but I'm really glad I pushed through to give this game a fair chance, because I'm honestly having a blast with it, and I expect it's something I'll come back to.

Coming here from Divinity OS2, I can say that this game is pretty good. Now to elaborate on that further;

Pros:
- The characters feel very much alive.
- Beautiful, vibrant world.
- Superb Voice Acting.
- The RPG part is actually in the game.
- It's DOS writing. Expect laughter, a lot of it and quite a few grim moments as well.
- It feels like a proper adventure. Slow burn of a story, I personally like it, but some people don't like stories that take it slow.
Cons:
- Slow animations for spells, running, etc. Makes the game feel a lot slower than it should.
- No out of combat health regen unless you've got cheese wheels in your backpack, unlike in Divinity OS2, where you can just rest on a bedroll.
- Combat encounter upon combat encounter upon combat encounter. Just a few too many of them.
- Camera angling in fights can often cause you to miss click the ground and walk instead of attack/do your chosen action.
- Dipped a toe in zappy water? Enjoy being stunned for three turns. Went on a patch of Ice? Enjoy being knocked down for 2 turns. You get stunned, paralyzed, petrified, knocked down, far too often, especially towards the end game, resulting in a very frustrating and tedious experience.

Would I still recommend it? Yeah. I would, even if there are some annoyances in the game, they're nothing you can't conquer with some coordination and [b]preparation.[/b]

I can't stress enough how great this game is. It's a unique title for the RPG genre, in my opinion. The combat has a vaguely similar feel of old style Dragon Age insofar as the bird's eye tactical view, but it's turn based in what reminds me of a Final Fantasy Tactics style, sans the grid. Each unit will act in a specific order (based on an individual character's speed and perception) and you have impeccable control over your environment. 

While the awesome combat mechanics are definitely what put this game beyond a lot of others in my eyes, the way you can approach quests, build your characters, employ clever gimmicks to solve puzzles, and generally interact with the game is unlike anything else I've come across in modern RPGs. The co-op is an experience, too, especially if you get a laugh out of screwing each other over in a round or two of combat. That can get really goofy, it's a good time. Oh, I should mention that the soundtrack is excellent, too.

I guess my only "complaint" about this game is that the story was good, but not the best I've ever come across. If not for the variety of ways you can influence your own experience, I might like it less. But really, the premise is good, the build-up is good, the primary cast of characters makes for an interesting introduction and progression. It's helped along a lot by some great voice acting and world-building. I was indifferent to some of the secondary protagonists though, and I ended up foregoing the companions altogether in my solo tactician playthrough. But I wanted a challenge, so it wasn't completely to do with the characters themselves.

Overall, Divinity: Original Sin - Enhanced Edition is a hell of an experience and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys RPGs and a more tactical style of combat.

This, along with the sequel is two of my top 10 games of all time.  Relatively unpopular opinion but I like this a little more than the sequel. These two games singlehandedly made me fall in love with turn based combat.

It's a very, very difficult recommend from me. The unfortunate thing about this game is that the sequel just does everything infinitely better. DOS:1 is not even required reading to enjoy or understand anything that's going on in DOS:2 as they only have the most minor and inconsequential of connections. This was Larian Studios first real crack at an RPG of this caliber and it shows. So many minor things just *grate*; the story is almost cartoonishly simple with crude humor, the gameplay is easily exploitable and rough around the edges and there's just so much dead time between animations that you really notice. Many times in the middle of combat you'll just sit there staring at some enemy take a century to choose a spell to cast and then waste even more time watching the animation play out. I mainly finished it out of slave-like obedience to my extreme autism and OCCD (Obsessive Compulsive Completionist Disorder). So, why am I recommending it at all? For two reasons; first, this game's existence is what kickstarted Larian (literally) and inspired them to create some genuine masterpieces. Everything that enabled their future successes was first iterated here in this entry in the tactical combat and world interactivity. Second, you can tell they just had so much fun making this game; it's something you can notice in the design, the voice-acting and all of the campiness. It's like a quirky DND game between friends. It's almost wholesome in that aspect but unfortunately by the end I was left feeling only a fraction of that enjoyment on my side.

I can’t pinpoint it exactly, but I never lost myself in the world completely … which is sad, because I really like those types of games and I wanted to like this game right till the end! A similar experience, but way less happened in Divinity 2. Maybe I need to watch some lore vids to dive deeper and then I enjoy the world of Divinity more …

A brilliant turn-based RPG that will probably drive you to unwittingly spend countless hours in long sessions and keep coming back for more; not perfect by any means, but still amazing. 

Pros:
-Interesting, engaging storyline and a thoroughly immersive world.
-Well-implemented, tactically satisfying combat system.
-Full voice acting that is really well done.
-Lovely soundtrack. 
-Pretty great co-op implementation; in fact, the game is probably better with a friend to get you through some of the more drawn-out parts. 
-Unrestricted character creation and progression, making for some fairly interesting builds.

Cons:
-The unrestricted character creation is a double-edged sword; you can absolutely end up with a weak build, and without easy access to respeccing it can be outright punishing (especially on higher difficulties). 
-Quest log is not particularly informative; you might have to look quests up online rather often, especially if you go longer between sessions.
-Quest progression might not be especially clear-cut and intuitive; you may find your progress hampered by reaching enemies that far outlevel you and end up having to backtrack a lot. 
-Pacing issues: it gets quite slow at times (again, co-op really helps with those!) and requires a fair bit of patience. 
-Inventory managing can be a hassle.
-Camera would benefit from the option to zoom out more.
-The ever-present occasional bugs and crashes.
